item.title: The Hazards of Marijuana
item.description:
Cannabis

The Hazards of Marijuana

We call marijuana “plant medicine,” but is it actually harmless?

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • Calling marijuana "plant medicine" implies it carries no risk of harm.
  • Heavy marijuana use has serious risks, and even light use is not risk-free.
  • Like any recreational drug, it's important for users to understand the risks of marijuana.

Marijuana has long been a popular drug. When it first became popular, it was seen as the drug of choice for “stoners”—people who drop out of school or life. People who lose motivation to do much of anything.

After its legalization, it’s become more popular, especially amongst adolescents and seniors. It has also become considerably stronger.

Not only that, but there’s a new trend to refer to it as “medicine.” It's been touted as a remedy for wide-ranging issues from pain to anxiety, sleep disorders, and a range of other physical and psychological issues.

Is Marijuana "Harmless"?

The problem is, public opinion has changed far faster than science. Many drugs are made from plants—alcohol and heroin, for example—as well as cocaine and mescaline. Like cannabis, these recreational drugs have potential “medicinal value.” However, all of them also have potentially serious consequences. When people solely refer to marijuana as “plant” and “medicine,” it makes it sound as if it’s unique amongst these drugs and without potential harm.

It isn’t. It is, in fact, a drug. And while, in the future, science may be able to truly isolate and research parts of the plant and its components and create medicine from it, in its current form it should be understood as a drug. And while many people use cannabis without catastrophic outcomes, research increasingly shows measurable risks—including addiction, psychosis, paranoia, cognitive effects, and worsening mental health—that deserve more public attention.

The Risks of Marijuana

For example, people are often surprised to learn that marijuana can be addictive. To be fair, when it first became popular in the 1960s, addiction was considerably more rare. But that marijuana was a different drug than today’s—much less potent. Today, statistics indicate that roughly 3 in 10 cannabis users develop some degree of cannabis use disorder, which can include cravings, withdrawal, loss of control, and continued use despite problems caused by using the drug. Risk of addiction rises substantially with daily use, and earlier age of onset (1 in 6 who begin use before 18) and the number has been rising each year.

In addition to addiction, there’s a strong—almost definitive—link between marijuana and psychosis/schizophrenia. While it’s impossible to prove causation, there’s a proven association between the two. The highest risk appears to be in genetically vulnerable individuals, but earlier use increases risk (the younger the user, the higher the probability of psychosis), as do higher THC potency and higher doses. That said, research now shows the risk exists even without any genetic predisposition. Symptoms can include paranoia, hallucinations, and increased schizophrenia risk. It’s called cannabis-induced psychosis.

There are even more common problems that can affect even recreational users. For example, there’s strong evidence that some users become markedly paranoid while intoxicated. Similarly, others experience irritability and anger during withdrawal from its effects. People are often surprised to hear this—the mellow, silly stereotype associated with marijuana doesn’t fit with symptoms of anger or rage. But a daily-life study found marijuana use was associated with increased impulsivity on the same and following days of use, and with greater interpersonal hostility the following day. In fact, heavy or frequent cannabis use is linked to much higher odds of physical violence.

No Use Is Risk-free

As stated earlier, most people can use marijuana lightly without serious harm. That said, even light, occasional use should not be confused with being “risk-free.” Cannabis is associated with impaired driving, attention and memory effects, anxiety (in people who are susceptible), and loss of motivation. Cannabis use has also been linked to decreased heart muscle contractility and vascular inflammation, and long-term recreational users show average IQ decline, with the effects especially concentrated in those who start young (before the age of 25).

Public perception largely views marijuana use as harmless. This is partly because of its former, less powerful history (as a more “lightweight drug”) but also because of the introduction of “medical marijuana,” social media portrayal, and, similar to alcohol, the normalization due to legalization. But the marijuana sold today is of a significantly higher THC potency than decades ago. Like alcohol, marijuana exists on a spectrum of risk. The problem is that public conversation increasingly focuses on the benefits while minimizing the documented harms.

item.title: The Psychological Perks of Hobby-Maxxing
item.description:
Happiness

The Psychological Perks of Hobby-Maxxing

Forget your career — let’s focus on your hobbies.

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows that engaging in hobbies is linked to fewer depressive symptoms and better physical health.
  • Being recognized for one's hobby can maximize its psychological perks.
  • Based on its benefits, the development of hobbies could be as important as the attention one puts on a career.
Rather than be a jack-of-all-trades, be a hoe-of-all-hobbies
Source: Lany Jade Mondou / Pexels

The other day, I saw a now-viral video in my feed that declared, “Forget being a jack-of-all-trades, I want to be a hoe-of-all-hobbies.” I loved the wordplay, sure, and didn’t make anything more of it.

But then at graduate school orientation the following week, during introductions when everyone had to go around the room and share what they liked to do for fun, every other person mentioned the same sentiment. Student after student described hobbying itself as a pastime: not just dabbling in one hobby or two, but sampling a variety of different ones.

Up until recently, I thought a hobby was like a job, or a personality trait: something that lasted over many seasons (or occasionally over a lifetime) and that said something fundamental about you. But now more than ever, when everything seems to be either outrageously expensive or falling apart, hobbying may take on a whole new meaning.

From Grandmacore to Whimsy-Maxxing, Hobbying is the Latest Trend That’s Actually Good for You

While back, Grandmacore brought back cozy vibes and the aesthetic decision to model oneself after your (hypothetical) grandmother’s cottage. Then “whimsy-maxxing” became a trend, which focused on bringing casual joys to everyday life, from fiction (my personal favorite) to thrifting. Maybe the internet likes to read into things too much, but both these other trends actually relate to the broader phenomenon of treating the small, pleasurable things in life as serious pursuits just as worthy of your time and energy as the big stuff, like your career.

After all, if there is one thing grandmothers are known for, it’s having a lot of hobbies. Tons of studies on the psychological importance of hobbies have focused exclusively on older adults in their 60s and up. Across countries, researchers have found that hobbies are good for you: They are linked to greater psychological and physical health, including, but not limited to, more happiness and life satisfaction, along with less depression.

How to Maximize the Benefits of Hobbying

That said, you can maximize the benefits of hobby-maxxing in one important way. Research on the link between engaging in hobbies and (fewer) depressive symptoms found that recognition played a key role in explaining the relationship. Among adults in the study, being recognized for your hobby could essentially account for why spending your free time doing something you love was so good for your well-being.

So in case you need empirical evidence to motivate you, don’t just do your hobby alone at home. Share it with a friend or stranger. Find a group of fellow hobbyists who love the same thing you do. Whatever strange, marvelous, or common thing you’re into, the internet has made it disgustingly easy to find other people who are similarly obsessed.

ComicCon is filled with people with day jobs but who have their priorities straight when it comes to hobbies
Source: Brent Singleton / Pexels

Last month, I went to Comic-Con San Diego—a yearly tradition I’ve started ever since becoming an author and finding myself on book panels at the convention. I confess I’m not a comics person, and the only cosplay I do involves national holidays that fall on the last day of October, so I’m not the prime demographic for the event. Still, I go back every year because there’s something magical about being in a convention center with over a hundred thousand other people who all have day jobs but are also passionate about how they spend their free time, whether it’s meticulously crafting the most intricate of costumes from scratch or designing their own board games.

I’ve always suspected (and now there is empirical proof): We just might be better off obsessing less about our careers and more about our hobbies.

item.title: The Diffusion of Responsibility and Pull of Conformity
item.description:
Conformity

The Diffusion of Responsibility and Pull of Conformity

Both of these phenomena get in the way of doing the right thing.

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • Diffusion of responsibility means that people sometimes don't act to help others, thinking someone else will.
  • Conformity also exerts a strong pull, causing people to shy away from doing or saying the right thing.
  • It is important to consider how one should respond when a person needs help before it occurs.

After extensively researching Holocaust history for my novel over the last two years, I've become much more aware of two related phenomena in social psychology: diffusion of responsibility and conformity. Both can hold individuals and groups back from doing the right thing.

Diffusion of responsibility

This phenomenon, also called the bystander effect, suggests that when someone is being harmed, the more witnesses present, the less likely anyone is to help or rescue them.

An oft-cited example is the case of Kitty Genovese in New York City in 1964, who shouted for help repeatedly while being assaulted on the street. No neighbor or bystander responded to help, and she was left to die on the street that day.

The bystander effect has since been examined in various social contexts. There are several reasons, some rational and some irrational, why otherwise well-meaning and moral people do not get involved to help a fellow citizen in danger.

Foremost, people don’t respond because they believe that someone else will.

They may feel unsure of their capacity to help or conclude that others would be more capable.

Or, they might hesitate to act to avoid accountability for their actions if they are unsuccessful. Or, they might simply refuse to put their own safety at risk.

On the darker end of the spectrum are those who hold a bias against the race, gender, or other trait of the victim. Their prejudice leads them to justify that the person, to some degree, deserves what is happening to them.

It is easy to excuse ourselves from rescuing someone in danger. That is why heroes are recognized as those who don’t make excuses, but rush in to help, risking their lives.

How does this look on a larger societal scale? How might it relate to the seemingly endless creep of atrocities that occurred in Germany from 1933 until the end of World War II? And how does it look today, when various groups of people are being openly victimized around the world?

Nazi Germany

Correspondence between my American grandmother and her Jewish German cousins in Berlin reveals that many persecuted Jews remained cautiously hopeful that someone, somewhere, somehow, would put an end to Hitler, his hateful ideology, and his abhorrent actions against them, before it was too late.

The non-Jewish Germans all around them fell into a few categories.

Some were fully aligned with the Reich, believing Hitler could fix the damaged economy and loss of cultural pride Germany still suffered in the aftermath of World War I.

If the Führer claimed Jews were to blame, so be it; they were more than willing to believe him. Millions supported his agenda with loud cheers and salutes or with silent assent.

A second category later claimed to have been unaware of the extent of the genocide until late in Hitler’s rule. However, a study by the UCL Centre for Holocaust Education indicated that awareness of Hitler’s actions against Jews was widespread early in 1942.

This brings to light the corporate responsibility of German citizens who did nothing to respond after pogroms like Kristallnacht in 1938, when persecution of Jews was plain for all to see. They regularly observed their fellow Germans, all Jews stripped of their citizenship, leave Germany on cattle cars, never to return.

It became unescapably clear that Hitler intended to eliminate all Jews throughout the expanding Reich, and if large numbers objected, they did nothing to oppose it. They were bystanders.

Righteous exceptions

There were a significant number of pro-Jewish, good-willed Aryans who believed strongly in the need to advocate for and protect their Jewish friends and neighbors, and some did take action. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, the Lutheran minister, was one example, and he paid for his support of Jews with his life.

But many sympathetic non-Jews didn’t act to defend Jews, even if they felt strongly convicted about it. In my novel, one of my grandmother’s cousins, Georg, has a frank conversation about this dilemma with Klaus, his Aryan business partner. Klaus says:

“I’ve lost sleep wondering what I’d do if the Gestapo came for you, or Luise, or Anna, or my other Jewish friends and colleagues. I’m not the bravest of men, but I’d like to think that I’d be able to speak up and do the right thing if that time came. Then I think about my wife and children, and feel like a coward. I ask myself if it’s right to risk the safety of my family to stand up for Jewish families…”

Klaus and Georg commiserate, both acknowledging their powerlessness. They could only hope that someone with real power would do something. Would it be the Lutherans, the military, some remnant of the former government, or a multiplicity of the German people?

Help didn’t come until the Allies declared war on Germany, and it took almost four more years to finally vanquish the Nazis, by which time over six million Jews had been killed.

Conformity

The perceived need to conform also prevents people from standing up for what is right. In a series of experiments by Solomon Asch in the 1950s, Asch demonstrated that subjects will give a knowingly wrong answer to an easy problem if all of the experimenter’s confederates give that answer first.

We can witness on film the inner struggle on the faces of the experimental subjects when all the confederates give false answers. When the subject is called upon, he must decide whether to say what his eyes tell him or deny reality and conform to the group consensus. A large percentage of subjects conformed.

Later, Asch modified the experiment, instructing one confederate to give the correct answer. When he did, the experimental subject became willing to give the correct answer. This supported the hypothesis that only one “truth-teller” was needed to encourage the subject to speak the truth.

What about us?

In real-world application, obviously the first person to buck the crowd is heroic, but the second person is also vitally important. The second person to act heroically or speak the truth represents a move against peer pressure, validating truth over lies. Two are better than one to fight a false or harmful consensus and influence others to join them.

This has huge implications in the fight against racism, antisemitism, and other injustices in our times.

We might ask, could I be the first person with the courage to defy group consensus or the bystander effect? Or could I be the second person, link arms with the first person, and call others to join us in protecting innocent victims or telling an unpopular truth when it matters the most?

item.title: With AI, How Much of You Is Left?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

With AI, How Much of You Is Left?

AI can make your work faster and more polished, but at what cost?

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • Overreliance on AI can distance people from their own ideas, judgments, and work.
  • AI can improve writing efficiency, but it can also make individual writing styles more similar.
  • AI-generated personal messages may be perceived as less sincere than human-written ones.
  • AI works best as an assistant, not as a substitute for human voice, ownership, or connection.

I recently had to call a local plumbing company. When they answered, I was pretty sure I was talking to AI. It was very human-like, certainly not robotic. But there was just enough peculiarity in the spacing between some words that made me think, “this is not a real person.” My immediate, visceral reaction was, “ick!”

It almost made me angry. I wanted to challenge the voice, demanding, “You aren’t even real, are you?!” While I was about 80 percent sure I was speaking to AI, the nagging 20 percent that maybe it was just an awkward human prevented me from saying something rude.

Reflecting on that experience made me examine how I use AI to help me wordsmith an email or create infographics and fliers. I’ve used AI to help my productivity in ways that may have detracted from my own unique, imperfect “humanness.”

And while generative AI can be an amazing tool, where’s the line between it being an amazing assistant and it going a little bit too far?

Three Things AI Can Quietly Take Away From Workplace Communications

Voice

Many people have turned to AI for crafting emails. It can do so quickly and efficiently with a polished feel.

AI can cause you to lose your voice in workplace communications.
Source: x_OI/Pixabay

Contrast this with a human experience. I remember one of my first times as chair of a hiring committee, when an unsuccessful candidate reached out asking for feedback. I wanted to be helpful, but I also needed to be careful about what I said. After consulting with HR, I spent close to an hour painstakingly crafting a response that was HR-compliant, and it offered real, actionable feedback while maintaining a friendly warmth.

Generative AI has changed that. What took me an hour (plus consultation with HR) to compose could now be drafted in seconds (and it was HR-compliant).

But there may be a tradeoff. A recent study examining more than 880,000 texts found that although AI writing assistance generally preserved the meaning of people’s writing, it also made writing styles more similar. Some linguistic individuality gets lost in the polishing process.

That’s the potential problem with handing these tasks over to AI. The message may be technically yours, but not the vocabulary, sentence structure, warmth, or level of formality. AI should make it easier to express your thoughts, not replace them. Have you read an email and thought: “I would never say that.”

Ownership

Recently, I attended an academic conference on evidence-based teaching and learning and heard colleagues lamenting about the ubiquitous use of generative AI at both the undergraduate and graduate level. Several people described students presenting beautiful research posters, with their work summarized perfectly, but then being completely unable to explain it in their own words.

It was like they’d outsourced the entire thing to AI. It created a beautiful product, but the students could not explain or defend it. They didn’t really understand what had been done or what the primary outcomes were.

While AI can be great at various stages of a project (early brainstorming or iterating on ideas; late-stage proofreading or formatting assistance), when the human operating the AI can’t articulate what happened or know the importance, it’s gone too far. There’s a difference between: “Here’s what I’m trying to say. Help me say it more clearly.”

And, “What should I say?”

Don’t turn your work entirely over to AI. If you use AI for assistance in a project, do a quick pulse check: Are these ideas, judgments, and sentiments my own? If not, it’s time to step in and revise.

Connection

Outsourcing relational communication is fraught. It might be a word of congratulations after a colleague’s promotion, or a condolence after a loss. If the primary purpose is connection, AI may misrepresent your intent.

Meaningful workplace connection can't be automated.
Source: StockSnap/Pixabay

A recently published study examined AI-generated birthday messages. Participants generally perceived AI-generated messages as being less sincere than human-written ones. Additionally, they liked the AI-written messages less and reported lower friendship satisfaction.

Some communication is about the thought and effort of reaching out itself. Taking a few moments to compose an email yourself is the whole point. You wouldn’t want to outsource it, because the entire point is to say, “I took the time and effort to reach out. You matter to me.”

The last thing you want is for someone who primarily interacts with you virtually to see you in person and feel like you have an entirely different persona than what is presented online. Whether it's your quirky sense of humor, overuse of exclamation marks, or the occasional inside joke or odd phrase, AI can’t replicate you.

The takeaway isn’t to stop using AI. Used well, generative AI can save time, help us brainstorm, improve clarity, and take some of the drudgery out of our work. Research even suggests that AI-assisted writing can sometimes help people communicate more effectively and efficiently.

But efficiency shouldn’t be the only goal of workplace communication. Our words convey who we are.

The best question is: “How much of me is left in the final product?” Does it sound like me? Are the ideas and judgments my own? And when the purpose is human connection, did I remain the core part of the interaction?

AI can polish an awkward sentence, soften a brisk tone, or organize scattered thoughts. It can even remind you when you’ve used one too many exclamation marks (although you’re certainly free to ignore it).

But the quirks, imperfections, humor, judgment, and effort that make communication distinctly yours aren’t necessarily problems to be optimized. Sometimes, they’re the whole point. Use AI as an assistant. Just make sure you’re still the person doing the communicating.

item.title: What Dolly Parton Taught Us About Being Our Authentic Selves
item.description:
Grief

What Dolly Parton Taught Us About Being Our Authentic Selves

The power of refusing to become what others expect us to be

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • So many are mourning Dolly Parton, showing how deeply artists can become part of our personal lives.
  • Dolly Parton’s voice, defiance, and sassy humor resonated with millions and made people feel less alone.
Dolly Parton
Source: Jack Fordyce / Shutterstock

“I'm not going to limit myself just because people won't accept the fact that I can do something else.”
—Dolly Parton

The loss of Dolly Parton feels enormous. For generations of people who grew up with her music, her humor, her voice, and her larger-than-life presence, her death can feel extremely personal. Around the world, people are grieving someone most never met, turning to the work she left behind, playing her songs, sharing favorite performances, and returning to the stories she told across a career that lasted more than six decades.

In many ways, art can become an emotional archive of experiences and feelings in our personal lives. A song outlives the moment in which it was created, and sometimes the person who created it.

The Myth of the Tortured Artist

We often romanticize the relationship between suffering and creativity. We latch onto the heartbreak that runs beneath an album, connect to the trauma that becomes a novel, or relate to the loss we see in a painting.

The creative process can help people externalize experiences that are difficult to articulate. Artistic expression may facilitate meaning-making and help people maintain an evolving connection with someone they have lost (Balan, 2023).

But that doesn’t mean grief automatically makes someone more imaginative. In fact, creative output may suffer during periods of acute grief. Trauma and pain can ignite the artistic process, but they can also disconnect us from ourselves and make it impossible to create (Balan, 2027).

One of Parton’s most famous songs, “I Will Always Love You,” emerged from loss.

When she decided to leave The Porter Wagoner Show and pursue a solo career, Wagoner resisted the decision. Parton felt unable to make him understand why she needed to leave.

So she did what she knew how to do.

She wrote a song about it.

“I Will Always Love You” became the goodbye she had been unable to communicate in conversation. Parton wrote it during an emotionally charged turning point while facing a decision that would change both of their lives.

Parton was sassy, funny, defiant, and remarkably real. There was an irreverence to the way she presented herself and a willingness to laugh at herself before anyone else got the chance. She was glamorous without taking glamour too seriously and ambitious without apologizing for wanting more.

Parton often met adversity with humor—and rarely let other people tell her who she was supposed to be. She understood that her exaggerated femininity could make people underestimate her, and she often seemed to enjoy being in on the joke.

Dolly Parton
Source: Carl Beust / Shutterstock

“I’m not offended by all the dumb blonde jokes because I know I’m not dumb—and I’m not blonde either.” —Dolly Parton

She famously turned judgments about class, beauty, and femininity into an identity she authored for herself. She openly traced her signature look to the woman her mother called the “town tramp,” recalling that her feeling was, “That’s what I want to be when I grow up. Trash.”

What others put down, Parton could reclaim and transform with creative defiance. “I would never stoop so low as to be fashionable,” she joked.

Then Parton Couldn’t Write

Decades later, when Parton’s husband, Carl Dean, died in March 2025 after nearly 60 years of marriage, she found herself having trouble writing.

Parton said ideas were still coming to her, but she wasn’t ready to finish them. Writing would require her to enter an emotional space she did not yet feel ready for.

A writer, musician, actor, painter, or performer often has to move toward emotions that the rest of us may instinctively move away from. They notice them, inhabit them, shape them, and eventually offer them to an audience. Acute grief can make that access overwhelming.

When Your Pain Is Also Your Profession

Most of us are allowed some separation between our grief and our work. Performers often aren’t. In the midst of difficult life events, a musician may still be expected onstage, an actor still has a call time, and a writer still has a deadline. The public figure may have interviews, appearances, contracts, employees, audiences, and an entire professional ecosystem that continues operating while their private world has changed.

People may wonder what the loss will produce or what the breakup will sound like on the next album. The performer may feel pressured to turn their pain into material. Suffering becomes not only personal experience but potential content.

Creativity Is Not Always Catharsis

We often talk about creativity as cathartic, but catharsis isn’t automatically therapeutic.

Making art can help people organize experience, create meaning, preserve connection, and communicate feelings that are difficult to put into ordinary language. But creative engagement with painful material can also evoke emotional overload. A person may need distance before they can create from an experience (Balan, 2023).

This may be particularly relevant for performers because their emotional expression does not remain private (Balan, 2027). Once transformed into a song, film, book, or performance, an intimate experience can become a product audiences consume, interpret, critique, and ask the artist to revisit repeatedly.

Parton was famous for her optimism, but she always made room for adversity rather than pretending it did not exist. “If you want the rainbow, you have to put up with the rain,” she said.

The Artist Behind the Work

Parton transformed poverty, longing, jealousy, separation, ambition, family, and love into stories other people could recognize themselves inside. Her autobiographical songwriting, from “Coat of Many Colors” to “I Will Always Love You,” helped make the deeply personal feel universal. People could find themselves in her humor, heartbreak, ambition, tenderness, and refusal to be anyone other than herself.

Parton once said, “Above everything else I’ve done, I’ve always said I’ve had more guts than I’ve got talent.” Talent matters, but creating also requires the courage to expose oneself, risk being misunderstood, and keep making things even when other people have already decided who you are supposed to be.

We do artists a disservice when we imagine that every wound should become art, or that creativity proves resilience. Sometimes resilience looks like recognizing that the pain is still too close to touch.

Parton’s extraordinary body of work reminds us that art can carry pieces of a person long after they are gone. Before there is the performer, the songwriter, the story, or the song, there is a human being experiencing the loss.

And perhaps the greatest respect we can offer an artist is to remember that their pain never owed us a performance. When they chose to share pieces of themselves through their art, they gave us something in return: a way to feel more understood, less alone, and more connected to one another.
